questions.stem: What does a reaction profile show?

options.text: The energy changes during the progress of a reaction, including activation energy and enthalpy change
The temperature change during a reaction
The concentration of reactants over time
The rate of reaction over time

questions.explanation: A reaction profile (also called an energy profile or reaction pathway diagram) shows how the energy of the system changes as the reaction progresses. It shows the activation energy, the transition state, and the overall enthalpy change.

questions.stem: What is the transition state (activated complex) on a reaction profile?

options.text: The starting energy of the reactants
The point where the reaction is complete
The highest energy point on the profile, where old bonds are partially broken and new bonds are partially formed
The energy level of the final products

questions.explanation: The transition state is the peak of the reaction profile. At this point, the reactant bonds are partially broken and the product bonds are partially formed. It represents the highest energy arrangement during the reaction.

questions.stem: On a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, what two measurements can be read?

options.text: Temperature and pressure
Activation energy (Ea) and enthalpy change (ΔH)
Mass and volume
Rate and concentration

questions.explanation: From a reaction profile, you can determine the activation energy (the energy difference between the reactants and the peak) and the enthalpy change (the energy difference between the reactants and the products).

questions.stem: How does a catalysed reaction profile differ from an uncatalysed one?

options.text: The catalysed profile has lower product energy
The catalysed profile has a higher peak
The catalysed profile has a lower peak (lower activation energy) but the same start and end energy levels
The catalysed profile has higher reactant energy

questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, shown as a lower peak on the profile. However, the energy levels of the reactants and products remain the same, so ΔH is unchanged.

questions.stem: A reaction profile shows reactants at 100 kJ, a peak at 250 kJ, and products at 50 kJ. What is the activation energy?

options.text: 100 kJ
50 kJ
200 kJ
150 kJ

questions.explanation: Activation energy = peak energy - reactant energy = 250 - 100 = 150 kJ. The activation energy is always measured from the reactant level to the peak, not from the product level.

questions.stem: Using the same reaction profile (reactants 100 kJ, peak 250 kJ, products 50 kJ), what is the enthalpy change?

options.text: -50 kJ
+50 kJ

questions.explanation: ΔH = energy of products - energy of reactants = 50 - 100 = -50 kJ. The negative value confirms this is an exothermic reaction (products have less energy than reactants).

questions.stem: Why does the reaction profile curve go upward before going downward in an exothermic reaction?

options.text: Because the products are formed before the reactants break apart
Because the temperature increases during the reaction
Because energy must first be put in to break existing bonds in the reactants before new bonds form and release energy
Because the catalyst makes the energy go up first

questions.explanation: The initial rise in the curve represents the activation energy needed to break the bonds in the reactant molecules. Only after this energy barrier is overcome can new bonds form in the products, releasing energy and causing the curve to drop below the starting level.
